IntroThe language of coordination chemistry

Decision flow
  1. Central metal atom/ion = Lewis acid (acceptor atom); ligand = Lewis base (has a donor atom)
  2. Ligands attached directly to the metal → inner-sphere complex (primary coordination sphere; their number = coordination number)
  3. Complex cation and anion merely associate electrostatically → outer-sphere complex

Complex: a central metal atom or ion surrounded by ligands. Coordination compound: a neutral complex, or an ionic compound in which at least one ion is a complex (e.g. [Ni(CO)₄], [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃).

Example: in a solution of [Mn(OH₂)₆]²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ the outer-sphere complex {[Mn(OH₂)₆]²⁺SO₄²⁻} can exceed the inner-sphere [Mn(OH₂)₅SO₄]. Uncoordinated water in a crystal = water of crystallization.

7.1Representative ligands

Decision flow
  1. How many points of attachment to the metal?
  2. One → monodentate
  3. Two → bidentate, three → tridentate … (together: polydentate)
  4. Two different potential donor atoms → ambidentate: e.g. NCS⁻ (κN / κS), NO₂⁻ (κN / κO)

A polydentate ligand forms a ring including the metal → a chelate. Normal chelating ligands bind only at two adjacent (cis) sites.

Example: en (1,2-diaminoethane) forms a five-membered ring. edta⁴⁻ is hexadentate (2 N + 4 O), giving a complex with five five-membered rings (used to trap Ca²⁺ in hard water).

β-Diketones (acac⁻ etc.) coordinate as enolate anions in six-membered rings. Chelate strain is expressed by the bite angle (L–M–L angle).

7.2Nomenclature

Decision flow
  1. For a salt, name the cation first, then the anion
  2. Within a complex ion: ligands in alphabetical order (ignore multiplying prefixes) → metal → oxidation number (Roman numerals) or charge
  3. Anionic complex → metal name + -ate (ferrate, cuprate, argentate, aurate, stannate, plumbate)
  4. Ligand name already contains a prefix → bis-, tris-, tetrakis- (e.g. tris(1,2-diaminoethane))
  • Bridging ligands: prefix μ (μ₃ for three metals). e.g. μ-oxido-bis(pentaamminecobalt(III))
  • Donor atom: κ (also number of attachments, κ²N); organometallic bonding modes: η
  • Formula: inside [ ] the metal, then ligands in alphabetical order of the binding element. e.g. [CoCl₂(NH₃)₄]⁺ = tetraamminedichloridocobalt(III)
ComplexName
[PtCl₂(NH₃)₄]²⁺tetraamminedichloridoplatinum(IV)
[Ni(CO)₃(py)]tricarbonylpyridinenickel(0)

7.3Low coordination numbers

Decision flow
  1. Three factors set the coordination number: size of the central atom / steric interactions between ligands / electronic interactions
  2. Large ions (later periods, left of a period), few d electrons → high coordination numbers (e.g. [Mo(CN)₈]⁴⁻)
  3. Electron-rich ions on the right of the d block, bulky ligands, multiply bonded ligands → low coordination numbers (e.g. [PtCl₄]²⁻, [MnO₄]⁻)

Coordination number 2: linear complexes of Group 11/12 ions such as Cu⁺ and Ag⁺ ($D_{\infty h}$). e.g. [AgCl₂]⁻, Me–Hg–Me. CuCN is really –Cu–CN–Cu– chains (CN 2).

Coordination number 3 is rare: found with bulky ligands, e.g. [Pt(PCy₃)₃] (trigonal planar, $D_{3h}$).

7.4Intermediate coordination numbers (4, 5, 6)

Decision flow
  1. CN 4: small central atom, large ligands (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) → tetrahedral ($T_\text{d}$)
  2. CN 4 with d⁸ (Rh⁺, Ir⁺, Pd²⁺, Pt²⁺, Au³⁺) → square planar ($D_{4h}$)
  3. CN 5: trigonal bipyramidal ($D_{3h}$) and square pyramidal ($C_{4v}$) differ little in energy → fluxional
  4. CN 6: almost always octahedral ($O_\text{h}$) or a small distortion of it

For 3d d⁸ (Ni²⁺), π-acceptor ligands (CN⁻) favour square planar: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻. A rigid ring of four donors (porphyrin) also enforces square planar.

Square-pyramidal geometry is enforced by porphyrins (myoglobin active site); trigonal-bipyramidal by tripodal ligands.

Six-coordination and its distortions

  • Tetragonal ($D_{4h}$): two trans ligands closer or further away. For d⁹ (Cu²⁺): the Jahn–Teller distortion
  • Rhombic ($D_{2h}$), trigonal ($D_{3d}$)
  • Trigonal prismatic ($D_{3h}$) is rare: MoS₂, WS₂, [Zr(CH₃)₆]²⁻. A chelate with a small bite angle distorts towards a trigonal prism

7.5Higher coordination numbers

Decision flow
  1. Larger atoms and ions → higher coordination numbers
  2. CN 7: pentagonal bipyramid ($D_{5h}$), capped octahedron, capped trigonal prism (rapid interconversion)
  3. CN 8: square antiprism and dodecahedron (cube is rare)
  4. CN 9 and above: mainly the f block (e.g. [Nd(OH₂)₉]³⁺; CN 12 [Ce(NO₃)₆]²⁻)

7.6Polymetallic complexes

Decision flow
  1. More than one metal atom
  2. Direct M–M bonds → metal cluster
  3. Linked only by bridging ligands → cage complex

7.7Square-planar complexes

Decision flow
  1. Isomers of MA₂B₂? Tetrahedral → one; square planar → two (cis / trans)
  2. Like ligands adjacent → cis ($C_{2v}$) / opposite → trans ($D_{2h}$)
  3. MABCD → three isomers

Werner isolated two isomers of [PtCl₂(NH₃)₂] → square planar. Only cis-Pt(II) complexes bind DNA long enough to work as anticancer drugs.

Chemical test: the cis isomer reacts with en (replacing two adjacent NH₃), the trans isomer does not react (en cannot span trans positions). ³¹P-NMR also distinguishes them.

7.8Tetrahedral complexes

Decision flow
  1. The only simple isomerism of tetrahedral complexes = optical isomerism
  2. All four ligands different, or two unsymmetrical bidentate ligands → chiral (not superimposable on its mirror image)

Two mirror-image isomers = an enantiomeric pair; they rotate polarized light in opposite directions (optically active).

7.9Trigonal-bipyramidal and square-pyramidal complexes

Decision flow
  1. Five-coordinate complexes are stereochemically nonrigid (fluxional) → isomers usually not separable
  2. Two sites in a trigonal bipyramid: axial (a) and equatorial (e)
  3. Two sites in a square pyramid: axial (a) and basal (b)

[Ni(CN)₅]³⁻ exists in both shapes in the same crystal. Interconversion: Berry pseudorotation.

7.10Octahedral complexes

Decision flow
  1. MA₄B₂ → cis ($C_{2v}$) / trans ($D_{4h}$)
  2. MA₃B₃ → mer (meridional, $C_{2v}$) / fac (facial, $C_{3v}$)
  3. MA₂B₂C₂ → five geometrical isomers (all-trans 1, one trans pair 3, all-cis enantiomeric pair)

(b) Chirality and optical isomerism

Decision flow
  1. No mirror plane or inversion centre (more generally no $S_n$ axis) → chiral
  2. Looking down a three-fold axis: clockwise helix → Δ (delta) / anticlockwise → Λ (lambda)
  3. Δ/Λ is the absolute configuration — not the same as the direction of optical rotation (d/l, (+)/(−))

Examples: [Mn(acac)₃] and [Co(en)₃]³⁺ are chiral. For [CoCl₂(en)₂]⁺ the cis isomer (violet) is chiral; the trans isomer (green) has a mirror plane and is achiral.

Resolution of enantiomers: form salts with an optically pure counter-ion (e.g. antimony d-tartrate) → diastereomers, separable by solubility.

7.11Ligand chirality

Decision flow
  1. A donor atom (e.g. N) that inverts rapidly in the free ligand becomes locked on coordination → a new chiral centre

Example: square-planar complex of MeNHCH₂CH₂NHMe → one chiral enantiomeric pair + two achiral forms = four isomers.

7.12Formation constants

Decision flow
  1. Large $K_\text{f}$ → the ligand binds more strongly than the solvent (H₂O)
  2. Stepwise constant $K_{\text{f}n}$: one replacement at a time
  3. Overall constant $\beta_n = K_{\text{f}1}K_{\text{f}2}\cdots K_{\text{f}n}$
  4. Dissociation constant $K_\text{d} = 1/K_\text{f}$: ligand concentration giving 50% complexation (same form as $K_\text{a}$)

Example: Fe³⁺ + SCN⁻ → [Fe(SCN)(OH₂)₅]²⁺ (red; test for Fe(III) or SCN⁻). $K_\text{f}$ spans a huge range, so it is quoted as log $K_\text{f}$.

7.13Trends in successive formation constants

Decision flow
  1. Usually $K_{\text{f}1} > K_{\text{f}2} > \cdots$ (fewer H₂O left to replace: statistical effect)
  2. Reversal or sudden drop → a major change in structure (or electronic structure)

For [Ni(NH₃)ₙ(OH₂)₆₋ₙ]²⁺, log $K_\text{f}$ = 2.72, 2.17, 1.66, 1.12, 0.63, 0.03 — a regular fall close to the statistical prediction (reaction enthalpies nearly constant).

  • [Fe(bpy)₃]²⁺ is far more stable than [Fe(bpy)₂(OH₂)₂]²⁺: change from high spin → low spin (larger LFSE)
  • Hg(II) halides: $K_{\text{f}3}$ anomalously low → change from six-coordinate to tetrahedral
  • Example 7.6: Cd²⁺–Br⁻ gives $K_{\text{f}4} > K_{\text{f}3}$ → change to tetrahedral releases three H₂O

7.14The chelate and macrocyclic effects

Decision flow
  1. Complex of a polydentate ligand vs the same number of monodentate ligands → polydentate is more stable
  2. Chelate effect is mainly entropic (number of independent molecules in solution increases)
  3. Macrocyclic effect = entropic effect + an enthalpic contribution from preorganization

Example: Cd²⁺ with one en ($K_\text{f1}$) vs two NH₃ ($\beta_2$): same two Cd–N bonds, but the chelate is favoured. More donor sites → bigger entropic advantage.

$K_\text{f}$ of 10¹² to 10²⁵ signals a chelate or macrocyclic effect. Also kinetically favoured (once one end binds, the other is close by).

7.15Steric effects and electron delocalization

Decision flow
  1. What size is the chelate ring?
  2. Five-membered → no strain, most stable
  3. Six-membered → fairly stable, favoured if electron delocalization occurs
  4. Three-, four-, seven-membered or larger → rare (angle strain, steric clashes)

Diimine ligands (bpy, phen) act as σ donors and as π acceptors: back-donation from filled metal $t_{2g}$ orbitals into empty ligand π* orbitals strongly stabilizes the complex (e.g. [Ru(bpy)₃]²⁺).

KCKey concepts summary

  • Complex = Lewis acid (metal) + Lewis bases (ligands); inner sphere vs outer sphere.
  • Monodentate, polydentate, ambidentate ligands; chelates bind at cis sites.
  • Naming: cation first; ligands alphabetical; anionic complex → -ate; bridging μ; donor atom κ.
  • CN 4: tetrahedral (small centre, large ligands) / square planar (d⁸). CN 5 is fluxional. CN 6 is almost always octahedral.
  • Isomerism: linkage, ionization, hydrate, coordination; geometrical (cis/trans, mer/fac); optical (Δ/Λ).
  • Formation constants: $\beta_n = \prod K_{\text{f}i}$; normally $K_{\text{f}n} > K_{\text{f}n+1}$, a reversal signals a structural change.
  • Chelate effect: mainly entropy; macrocyclic effect adds an enthalpic term.
